title: Pseudo atrioventricular block most likely caused by junctional extrasystoles mimicking Mobitz II second degree atrioventricular block: A case report
case_prompt: A 56-year-old man with hypertension presented with palpitations that had gradually increased in frequency over 6 months, particularly during physical activity, but without impact on his daily life. On examination, his pulse intermittently rose to 105 beats per minute with occasional pauses, findings corroborated by cardiovascular auscultation. A resting 12-lead ECG showed a junctional rhythm. A 24-hour Holter monitor demonstrated predominantly sinus rhythm with runs of junctional rhythm and episodes in which some sinus P waves failed to conduct to the ventricles. During treadmill exercise testing, in the fourth minute of exertion, two consecutive sinus P waves were nonconducted to the ventricles, with the PR interval before and after these nonconducted beats remaining unchanged at 160 ms, thereby mimicking a Mobitz II second-degree atrioventricular block.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Mobitz II second-degree atrioventricular block was initially suspected because “The pre- and postblock PR intervals with the same durations during an exertion phase of a stress test usually make Mobitz II second-degree atrioventricular block the main suspected diagnosis.”  
2. A true Mobitz II block in the absence of bundle branch block was deemed unlikely since “Mobitz II second-degree atrioventricular block in the absence of a bundle branch block is an uncommon condition found in less than 30% of cases.”  
3. A 1:2 conduction phenomenon via a slow pathway was considered but found less plausible because “it is unlikely that conduction through a fast pathway will switch to a slow one during atrial activation with fixed coupling interval in the absence of significant modulation of the autonomic nervous system.”  
4. Intranodal conduction delay was entertained but excluded given that “intranodal conduction delay could be a possibility; however, the presence of atrioventricular dissociation at certain moments excludes this hypothesis.”
